understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call measuring yourself against others, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: Seven days from comparing himself to everyone ahead to finding the one thing he can still do with his own hands and mind.

week_beats.diagnose: You see that it is the picture of everyone else ahead, not the rejections, that keeps you up.
week_beats.steady: You hold that the rejections are not a verdict, and that your path is your own.
week_beats.act: You try one practice that is yours to do: close the feed, name one thing learned, and do one thing today.
week_beats.story: A young man who sent his work into the world and was met with silence shows you how to keep your own measure.

understanding.mirror: Two hundred applications, and the feed shows everyone else already landed.

queries.hook: The weight of being left behind while everyone else is already ahead, and the shame of the flat white and the rejections.
queries.diagnose: Comparison and envy grow at another's success; measuring your life against theirs steals the contentment in your own and turns effort into anxiety.
queries.steady: The path you are walking is your own; the rejections are not a verdict on your worth, only the outcome you cannot yet control.
queries.act: Walk your own path, even imperfectly, rather than someone else's well; be grateful for what is yours and rejoice in others' good.
queries.story: A young man who sent his work into the world and was met with silence, who measured himself against those who were heard and found a way to keep his own measure.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse.sanskrit: श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् । स्वभावनियतं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम् ॥
verse.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.
verse.why: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.
verse.misuse: Not 'stick to the role you were born into'. It's about honest fit with your own nature, not caste or family script.

prasang.title: Duties by nature, and their fruit
prasang.summary: After listing duties by varna, Krishna says one reaches perfection through one's own work done as worship, and that one's own path, though imperfect, beats another's, since every undertaking has flaws.
prasang.lesson: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.

verse.meaning: Krishna is telling Arjuna that it is better to do your own work, even if it is imperfect, than to do someone else's work perfectly. He says that doing the work that fits your own nature means you do not incur any wrong. The point is to do what matches who you are, flaws and all, and offer it up.
verse.for_you: You have sent out your applications. You are making flat whites. These are your hands and your work right now. Do this work that fits you, imperfectly, as an offering. It is enough.

verse.speaker: Kakbhushundi
verse.setting: Kakbhushundi continues listing the diseases of the mind.
verse.sanskrit: ममता दादु कंडु इरषाई। हरष बिषाद गरह बहुताई॥ पर सुख देखि जरनि सोइ छई। कुष्ट दुष्टता मन कुटिलई ॥
verse.line: Envy is an itch. Burning at another's happiness is a wasting disease of the mind.
verse.translation: Possessiveness is ringworm and envy is the itch; the swings of elation and dejection are throat ailments. The burning you feel at another's happiness is consumption, and malice and a crooked mind are leprosy.
verse.why: Know your mind's diseases by name: confusion, anger, greed, envy, ego.

prasang.title: Garuda's seven questions
prasang.summary: Garuda asks seven questions: the rarest body, the greatest sorrow and joy, the nature of good and wicked people, the highest virtue and the worst wrong, and the diseases of the mind. Kakbhushundi answers: no sorrow like want, no joy like meeting good people; non-harm is highest and slander worst; delusion is the root disease, with lust, greed, anger, envy and ego as its symptoms.
prasang.lesson: Know your mind's diseases by name: confusion, anger, greed, envy, ego.

verse.meaning: Kakbhushundi is telling Garuda that envy is an itch and a wasting disease. He says that burning at another person's happiness is like consumption. The point is to know your mind's diseases by name. You can see confusion and envy for what they are.
verse.for_you: The picture of your friends at top firms is an itch. It burns at your own path. Name it as envy. See it as a disease of the mind, not a truth about your life.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how the wise live and work.
verse.sanskrit: यदृच्छालाभसन्तुष्टो द्वन्द्वातीतो विमत्सरः । समः सिद्धावसिद्धौ च कृत्वापि न निबध्यते ॥
verse.line: Content with what comes, beyond envy, steady in success and failure, you stay free even while working.
verse.translation: Content with whatever comes unasked, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy, the same in success and failure, even when acting he is not bound.
verse.why: Contentment and freedom from envy let you work without being bound.

prasang.title: How the great yogis live
prasang.summary: The wise act without selfish motive, content and dependent on nothing, free from envy, steady in success and failure.
prasang.lesson: Contentment and freedom from envy let you work without being bound.

verse.meaning: Krishna tells Arjuna that the wise are bound by nothing. They accept whatever comes without asking. They are free from envy. They remain the same in success and failure. They do not cling to the results of their work.
verse.for_you: You are making flat whites and sending out applications. That is your work for today. Let the rejections come and go. They do not decide your worth, and they do not decide your path.

verse.speaker: Ribhu
verse.setting: Ribhu on the mark of the wise.
verse.sanskrit: अनागतानां भोगानामवाञ्छनमकृत्रिमम् । आगतानां च संभोग इति पण्डितलक्षणम् ॥
verse.line: Not pining for pleasures still to come, and enjoying the ones already here: that is wisdom.
verse.translation: Not longing for pleasures yet to come, and enjoying those that have come: this, unforced, is the mark of the wise.
verse.why: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

prasang.title: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.
prasang.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

verse.meaning: Ribhu tells Nidagha that a free person does not pine for what is missing. They enjoy what is already here. They let go of what is lost. They take up what comes next. They do their work calmly inside.
verse.for_you: Your friends have landed at top firms. That is what is already here. You do not need to add to it by looking at what comes next. Do your work, enjoy the morning, and let the rest wait.

verse.speaker: Dharmavyadha (the righteous meat-seller)
verse.setting: In Mithila, a meat-seller famed for wisdom teaches a proud ascetic what goodness really is.
verse.sanskrit: अनसूयुः कृतज्ञश्च कल्याणान्येव सेवते / सुखानि धर्ममर्थं च स्वर्गं च लभते नरः
verse.line: Let go of envy and stay grateful, and good things keep finding their way to you.
verse.translation: The person who is free of envy and grateful keeps to what is good, and finds happiness, right living, prosperity and heaven.
verse.why: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.

verse.speaker: Kalakavrikshiya
verse.setting: The sage warns the deposed prince against resenting others' success.
verse.sanskrit: सहस्व श्रियमन्येषां यद्यपि त्वयि नास्ति सा / अन्यत्रापि सतीं लक्ष्मीं कुशला भुञ्जते नराः / अभिनिष्यन्दते देही श्रीभूतश्च द्विषज्जनात्
verse.line: Make peace with other people's success, even when you lack it. The wise can enjoy good fortune that isn't theirs.
verse.translation: Bear the good fortune of others, even though it is not with you. Wise people know how to enjoy good fortune even when it belongs to someone else; good fortune drains away from the one who resents.
verse.why: Grief can't restore what's gone. Want what's within reach, and let others' success be.

story.title: The senses argue over who is greatest
story.story_hook: One day the senses got into an argument about which of them mattered most.
story.summary: Speech, sight, hearing and mind each claim to be the most important. Their father says the greatest is the one whose absence hurts the body most. Each leaves for a year and the body manages; when breath starts to leave, all the others are torn loose and beg it to stay.
story.lesson: The quiet one everyone relies on often matters most.

anchor.speaker: Prajapati
anchor.setting: The senses quarrel over which of them is greatest.
anchor.sanskrit: अथ ह प्राणा अहꣳश्रेयसि व्यूदिरेऽहꣳश्रेयानस्म्यहꣳ श्रेयानस्मीति ॥ ते ह प्राणाः प्रजापतिं पितरमेत्योचुर्भगवन्को नः श्रेष्ठ इति तान्होवाच यस्मिन्व उत्क्रान्ते शरीरं पापिष्ठतरमिव दृश्येत स वः श्रेष्ठ इति ॥
anchor.line: The senses argued over who was greatest. The answer: the one whose absence hurts the whole body most.
anchor.translation: The senses quarrelled about who was best, each saying, 'I am best, I am best.' They went to their father Prajapati and asked, 'Sir, who is the best of us?' He said, 'The one whose departure leaves the body looking worst off is the best among you.'
anchor.why: The quiet one everyone relies on often matters most.

story.for_you: You spend hours on your phone seeing your friends ahead. You measure your flat whites and rejections against their top firms. But the mind that does this measuring is not your greatest strength. The quiet one that actually keeps you going is your own steady breath.

script: You are sitting with your phone and the rejections keep arriving. You keep looking at your friends and the places they have reached. You feel behind and ashamed. The picture of everyone else ahead is loud right now. It makes your own path look like a failure before you have even finished walking it.
Krishna is walking with Arjuna. He is looking at the armies arrayed on the field. Arjuna is filled with grief and confusion. He is asking why he must fight. And Krishna replies:
श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात्, स्वभावनियतं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम्.
In plain words: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.

Krishna is saying that your own duty, even if it has flaws and you stumble, is better than someone else's work done perfectly. He is talking about the work that fits your own nature. This is not about the role you were born into. It is about finding the honest work that is yours. Doing that work means you do not incur any wrong. The flaw is not in the work. It is in trying to be someone else.
You sent out your applications. You are making flat whites. These are your hands and your work right now. Do this work that fits you, imperfectly, as an offering. It is enough.
Whose path are you walking today?

depth.life: You are making flat whites and checking your phone. Your mother tells the aunties you are fine, but you feel the weight of every rejection. You see your friends landing jobs and you feel behind, as if your own path is a failure.
depth.points: The texts point to the root cause of this pain. It is not the rejections. It is the measuring of your own steps against the path of others. That comparison makes your own work look like a failure before it is finished.
depth.practice: Put the phone down and notice the steam rising from the milk. Feel the weight of the pitcher in your hand for one full minute.
depth.question: What does your own path look like when you stop looking at theirs?
